l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus first laments old age and praises Hercules, then celebrates the downfall of Lycus and the return of hope. At the end, it becomes alarmed by a spectre hovering over the palace and fears that new evils are approaching.

l: gods, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The gods are invoked as powers who hear holy prayers, recognize broken trust, and eventually restore neglected laws through punishment. The Chorus also praises Apollo and the divine associations of Hercules.

l: Thebes, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Thebes is ruled by Lycus after a revolt, and its people are threatened by the violence and disorder surrounding his seizure of power. The Chorus later celebrates the restoration of the rightful king and the city’s renewed joy.

l: the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The Underworld is the realm from which Hercules returns after a prolonged stay. Hercules says that he brought the three-headed dog into the light and rescued Theseus from the shades.

l: the Labours of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Hercules recalls fighting the Hydra and the lion and carrying out Eurystheus’s commands. He declares that such labours would not make him victorious if he failed to prevent the deaths of his own children.

l: Hercules’ return from the Underworld, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Hercules returns from the Underworld before Eurystheus knows that he has come back. He first goes to his household gods, bringing Cerberus from the Underworld and having rescued Theseus.

l: the attempted execution of Megara, Amphitryon, and the children, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Lycus orders Megara, Amphitryon, and the children to appear so that they may die by their own hands. Their execution is prevented when Hercules returns, hides in the palace, and confronts Lycus.

l: the death of Lycus, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: Lycus enters the palace intending to bring out Megara and the children, but Hercules ambushes and kills him. The Chorus hears his cries and celebrates his death as deserved.

l: Justice, Hecuba and other plays, HERCULES, MEGARA, AMPHITRYON, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus presents Lycus’s death as repayment for his violence, blasphemies, and unjust rule. It says that the gods recognize broken trust and restore neglected laws through vindictive punishment.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Iris and the Fiend conspire at Juno’s command to drive Hercules into madness and make him kill his children and Megara. The Fiend enters Hercules’ house, while the Chorus foresees disaster and a Messenger recounts how Hercules, believing his family to be Eurystheus’ children, kills them and Megara before Athena stops him. Hercules awakens bound among the corpses, learns what he has done from Amphitryon, and considers suicide, while awaiting the arrival of Theseus.

l: Iris, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Iris identifies herself as the gods’ ambassadress and declares that she and Juno intend to punish Hercules by driving him to kill his children. She commands the Fiend to instil frenzy in Hercules and then leaves for Olympus while the Fiend enters his house.

l: Fiend, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: The Fiend says that she is the daughter of Night and that she would dissuade Iris and Juno from attacking Hercules, whom she recognizes as a benefactor of the gods. Forced to obey, she enters Hercules’ house, vows to unleash terrible madness, and causes the slaughter before Athena checks Hercules’ violence.

l: Chorus of Theban old men, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus laments that Hercules, Greece’s benefactor and son of Jove, is about to be overwhelmed by an infernal frenzy. It mourns the deaths of his children and Megara, helps Amphitryon guard Hercules after the murders, and condemns Jove and the gods for allowing his suffering.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Hercules is driven mad by the Fiend and mistakes his own children for the children of Eurystheus, killing them and Megara with his weapons. Athena stops him by striking him with a rocky fragment, after which he is bound to a pillar; on waking, he learns of the murders and is overcome by grief, shame, and thoughts of suicide.

l: Jove, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Jove is identified as Hercules’ father, and the Chorus calls him mighty Jove. The Chorus asks why Jove has hated his son and allowed him to be plunged into such troubles.

l: Juno, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Juno is presented as the power directing vengeance against Hercules. She sends the Fiend with Iris to drive him mad and stain his hands by making him kill his family.

l: gods, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: The gods are said to have received their ancient honours again through Hercules after he established peace and restored order in lands and seas. Iris and the Fiend also argue that the gods would lose their power and authority if Hercules escaped punishment.

l: Amphitryon, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Amphitryon witnesses the devastation and grieves over the murdered children and Megara. He fears that Hercules may kill him as well, but after Hercules wakes he cautiously explains that Hercules, driven by madness, committed the murders.

l: Megara, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Megara is present with Hercules, Amphitryon, and the children during the purification ceremony. Hercules kills her and a child with a single shaft while in his madness.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ children are brought to the altar during the purification ceremony and become terrified when their father turns violent. They flee and hide, but Hercules kills all three, believing them to be Eurystheus’ children.

l: murder of Hercules’ children and Megara, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: The murder occurs after Hercules is seized by madness during a purification ritual. He kills his three children and Megara with his arrows and club before Athena interrupts his attack and he is bound while unconscious.

l: Hercules’ madness, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ madness is caused by the Fiend under the direction of Iris and Juno. It makes him mistake his father for Eurystheus’ father, imagine himself fighting and traveling to Mycenae, and murder his children and Megara before awakening without memory of the acts.

l: Theseus, Hecuba and other plays, IRIS, A FIEND, CHORUS.
s: Theseus has not yet appeared in this unit, but Hercules expects him to come as a kinsman and friend. Hercules believes Theseus may prevent him from acting on his desperate thoughts and may see the truth of his pollution and grief.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Theseus arrives with Athenian youths to help Hercules, but finds Hercules after he has killed his children and wife in a divinely induced frenzy. Hercules laments his suffering, rejects the gods, and considers death because he expects exile and universal pollution. Theseus persuades him to live, offers him refuge and wealth in Athens, and promises purification and honor. Hercules agrees to leave for Athens after Amphitryon buries the children, while Theseus leads him away as a steadfast friend.

l: Theseus, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Theseus brings an armed squadron of Athenian youths to assist Hercules, but arrives after the slaughter. He comforts Hercules, rejects the idea that friendship can transmit pollution, offers him refuge and wealth in Athens, and promises to obtain purification and honor for him. He finally leads Hercules away from Thebes.

l: Amphitryon, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Amphitryon tells Theseus that Hercules, seized by frenzy, killed his own children and wife. He urges Hercules to restrain himself and later agrees to bury the children. He asks who will bury him, and Hercules promises to do so after the burial.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules is found mourning and ashamed after killing his children and wife during a frenzy. He believes that his sufferings, pollution, and expected exile make life impossible, but Theseus persuades him to endure and accompany him to Athens. Hercules agrees to live, retain his weapons, and leave Thebes after Amphitryon performs the burial.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ children are dead after being killed by their father in his frenzy. Amphitryon is to bury them, since Hercules says the laws do not allow him to perform that office. Hercules mourns them and asks that their tomb be visited and lamented.

l: Megara, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ wife is among those killed in the disaster. Hercules mourns her as the woman who preserved his bed inviolate and watched over his house.

l: Juno, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Juno is identified as the cause of Hercules’ frenzy and destruction. Hercules says that her hatred began because of his birth from a woman loved by Jove, and that she has achieved her wish by destroying him and his household.

l: gods, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: The gods are blamed and questioned in the discussion of Hercules’ suffering. Hercules doubts that true gods would need support or be bound by the lawless marriages and crimes attributed to them, while Theseus warns him not to speak presumptuously against them.

l: Athens, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Athens offers Hercules refuge after his exile from Thebes. Theseus promises that Athens will cleanse him from pollution, provide him with a palace and wealth, and honor his memory after death.

l: Thebes, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Thebes is the city from which Hercules must depart because the laws exclude him after the killings. Hercules asks its citizens to mourn his children and himself, while Theseus leads him away toward Athens.

l: Hercules’ madness, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules’ madness seizes him after he is sprinkled with the venom associated with the hundred-headed hydra. In that frenzy he kills his own children and wife, then recovers sufficiently to understand and mourn what he has done.

l: murder of Hercules’ children and Megara, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: The murder occurs during Hercules’ frenzy and leaves the floor covered with corpses. Hercules regards it as the greatest of his sufferings and asks Amphitryon to bury the children because he cannot perform the rite himself.

l: the Labours of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules recalls his many labours, including killing lions, Typhons, giants, centaurs, and the hydra, and bringing the three-headed dog from the realm of the dead. He says that these labours were less painful than the present disaster.

l: Hercules’ exile, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules expects to be driven from his native Thebes and fears that no city or friend will accept him because of the killings. Theseus tells him to leave with him for Athens, and Hercules agrees to do so.

l: the burial of Hercules’ children, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Amphitryon is instructed to consign the children’s bodies to the tomb and shed the required tears. Hercules says that their mother should embrace them in death, while he will later return to take Amphitryon to Athens.

l: purification from pollution, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Theseus promises that Hercules’ hands will be cleansed from pollution in Athens. This purification is presented as part of the refuge and assistance Athens will provide.

l: pollution, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules calls himself a source of contagion after killing his children and fears that no one will speak to him or allow him to enter a city. Theseus rejects the idea that a friend can transmit harm to another friend and offers to share Hercules’ condition.

l: friendship, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Theseus demonstrates friendship by coming to help Hercules despite his misfortune and by offering him refuge, wealth, purification, and lasting honor. Hercules concludes that a steadfast friend is more valuable than wealth or dominion.

l: suffering and misfortune, Hecuba and other plays, THESEUS, AMPHITRYON, HERCULES, CHORUS.
s: Hercules describes his suffering as greater than any previous labour and believes that no human being has endured more. Theseus answers that no person escapes the wounds of fortune and urges Hercules to bear what the gods have inflicted.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Iolaus brings the children of Hercules to the altar of Jupiter at Marathon after Eurystheus has pursued them from city to city and sought their destruction. Copreus arrives from Argos to seize the children, but Demophoon and the Chorus of Athenian old men defend their right to remain as suppliants. Demophoon refuses to surrender them, invoking the gods, kinship, past services, and the shame of violating the altar. Copreus threatens to return with Eurystheus and an Argive army, prompting Demophoon to prepare Athens for war.

l: Iolaus, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Iolaus protects the children of Hercules after their father’s death, sharing their exile despite needing protection himself. At Marathon, he brings them to the altar of Jupiter and appeals to Demophoon and the Athenians to prevent their forcible surrender. He refuses to leave the altar until Demophoon has safely resisted the Argive threat.

l: Copreus, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Copreus comes from Argos as Eurystheus’ herald to seize the children of Hercules and return them to Mycene. He argues that Argos may execute its own subjects and threatens Athens with war, but Demophoon rejects his demands. Copreus withdraws, declaring that he will return with an armed Argive force.

l: Demophoon, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Demophoon hears the claims of Copreus and Iolaus and refuses to permit the children of Hercules to be dragged from the altar. He cites reverence for Jupiter, family ties, past services from Hercules, and the dishonor of surrendering suppliants through fear. He summons the citizens, prepares troops and seers, and promises to defend the suppliants.

l: Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Eurystheus has pursued Iolaus and the children of Hercules from city to city and sent Copreus to bring them back. He waits near Alcathous’ realm and threatens Athens through the promised arrival of an Argive army under his command.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Hercules is dead and is said to dwell in heaven. Iolaus formerly shared his labors, while his children now suffer exile and persecution because of their connection to him. Hercules is also remembered as having rescued Theseus from the caves of Pluto.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The children of Hercules are exiles pursued by Eurystheus, who seeks to seize and kill or otherwise punish them under an Argive decree. They sit as suppliants at the altar of Jupiter at Marathon under Iolaus’ protection. Demophoon refuses to surrender them and prepares to defend them against Argos.

l: Chorus of Athenian old men, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The Chorus discovers Copreus using force against Iolaus and the children of Hercules and declares that the suppliants of the gods must be protected. It supports Demophoon’s refusal to surrender them and warns that Argos’ threatened invasion requires careful preparation.

l: Argives, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The Argives, represented by Copreus and Eurystheus, demand the return of the children of Hercules and threaten Athens with armed conflict. Their forces are described as numerous and fierce, and Copreus announces that they will advance against Athens if the children are protected.

l: Athenians, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The Athenians are portrayed as a free people who honor the gods and protect helpless suppliants. Demophoon expects them to resist Argos rather than surrender the children of Hercules, and he prepares their forces for the threatened conflict.

l: Marathon, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Marathon is the city in the Athenian dominions where the action takes place. The children of Hercules and Iolaus seek refuge there at the altar of Jupiter.

l: Athens, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Athens is described as a free city whose rulers must not yield to Argive threats. Demophoon declares that Athens will not treat itself as an appendage of Argos and will defend the suppliants.

l: Argos, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Argos is the power from which the children of Hercules have been expelled or pursued. Through Copreus and Eurystheus, it demands their surrender and threatens Athens with invasion if its demand is refused.

l: Mycenae, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Mycene is ruled by Eurystheus, who sends Copreus to recover the children of Hercules. Copreus claims that Mycene may execute its own subjects, while Iolaus argues that the exiled children are foreigners there and cannot justly be dragged back.

l: altar of Jupiter, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The altar of Jupiter at Marathon provides the children of Hercules and Iolaus with sacred protection. Copreus attempts to remove them by force, but the Chorus and Demophoon declare that no one may violate the altar or drag suppliants from it.

l: Argive invasion of Athens, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The threatened Argive invasion of Athens follows Copreus’ failure to seize the children of Hercules. Copreus promises that Eurystheus and a large force will attack, and Demophoon begins gathering troops, spies, seers, and sacrificial victims to meet them.

l: exile of the children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The children of Hercules have been driven from their homeland and repeatedly expelled from places where they sought refuge because Eurystheus pursues them. Iolaus leads them to the Athenian realm, where they seek protection from further exile.

l: supplication at the altar, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Iolaus and the children of Hercules sit before the altar of Jupiter with sacred branches and wreaths, asking not to be surrendered or forcibly removed. Their supplication is recognized by the Chorus and Demophoon as a claim that the gods and the laws of Athens must protect.

l: execution decree against the children, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Copreus claims that the laws of Argos ordered the children of Hercules to bleed and that he has come to enforce that sentence. Iolaus counters that the children were banished from their native land and therefore cannot justly be reclaimed as its subjects.

l: protection of the suppliants, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: Demophoon undertakes to protect the children of Hercules from Eurystheus and refuses to let Copreus remove them. He treats their protection as required by the gods, kinship, gratitude for Hercules’ services, and the honor of Athens.

l: freedom of Athens, Hecuba and other plays, THE CHILDREN OF HERCULES.
s: The freedom of Athens is connected with its refusal to surrender suppliants through fear of Argos. Demophoon declares that Athens will maintain its independence rather than become an appendage of the Argive realm.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Demophoon reports that Eurystheus and the Argive army are approaching Athens, while the oracles require the sacrifice of a noble-born maiden to save the city and the foreign suppliants. Demophoon refuses to sacrifice his own daughter or any Athenian citizen, and Iolaus laments that the suppliants may be expelled. Macaria voluntarily offers herself as the victim so that her brothers and Athens may be saved, then departs for the sacrifice. A servant announces that Hyllus is leading an Athenian force into battle, and Iolaus insists on joining the fight despite his extreme old age.

l: Demophoon, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Demophoon reports that Argos, led by Eurystheus, is approaching with numerous troops. He has armed the city, arranged sacrifices and lustrations, and refuses to kill his daughter or compel an Athenian citizen to serve as the victim. He asks for a way to save both the country and the foreign suppliants without losing the citizens’ respect.

l: Iolaus, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Iolaus learns that the oracles demand the sacrifice of a noble-born maiden and fears that the suppliants will be surrendered. He proposes that the sisters draw lots, but accepts Macaria’s voluntary choice to die. When Hyllus’s attendant announces the approaching battle, Iolaus obtains armor and insists on going to fight despite his weakened body.

l: Macaria, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Macaria comes from her chamber after hearing Iolaus’s lament and voluntarily offers herself as the victim. She rejects selection by lot, saying that a free choice will preserve her merit, and asks to be conducted to death with proper rites. She entrusts her brothers and Alcmena to the survivors and requests that her brothers later honor her burial.

l: Alcmena, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Alcmena is described as the aged mother of Hercules and the grandmother of the children. She fears that an Argive herald has come to seize them, but learns that Hyllus is approaching with forces. She relies on the foreign suppliants and worries about being saved if Iolaus and the children are overcome.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Hercules is identified as the father of the children and the companion whose memory makes them targets of Eurystheus. Macaria invokes his name with pride and says that her conduct must be worthy of the father from whom she descends. Iolaus recalls fighting beside Hercules when he laid waste to the Spartan realms.

l: Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Eurystheus leads the Argive forces toward Athens and observes the routes by which his troops may attack. Macaria says that he seeks the death of the children because they are the offspring of a noble race and remember their father’s wrongs. Iolaus also describes him as unwilling to face the dangers of the battlefield.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus hopes that Jove will help Athens protect the hapless strangers and praises Macaria’s willingness to die for her brothers and the land. It sings that human prosperity and suffering change according to destiny, and invokes Earth, the Moon, Hyperion, Minerva, and the gods for victory over the Argive threat.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The children of Hercules are threatened with capture and death by Eurystheus. Macaria offers herself so that they may live, entrusts them to Iolaus, and asks them to revere Iolaus and Alcmena. Their welfare is presented as the reason for her sacrifice and for the conflict with Argos.

l: Argos, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Argos approaches Athens with numerous squadrons under Eurystheus. Its forces have not yet invaded the territory when Demophoon reports their position, but they are close enough for their leader to be distinguished.

l: Athens, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Athens is preparing to defend the foreign suppliants against Argos. Its city is armed, sacrifices and lustrations are performed, and its people are divided between aiding the strangers and criticizing Demophoon’s policy. The Chorus declares that Athens would be disgraced if it betrayed its guests.

l: gods, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The gods are invoked for protection, victory, and guidance in the crisis. Jove is said to chastise the presumptuous and to remain mindful of Alcmena’s sufferings, while Minerva is honored as the guardian of the land. The gods’ responses determine that a noble-born maiden must be sacrificed.

l: the oracles, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The oracles give differing instructions on the city’s situation, but all the relevant auspices agree that Ceres requires the sacrifice of a blooming maiden born to a noble father. Their response creates the crisis that Demophoon and the suppliants must resolve.

l: Athenian army, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The Athenian army is assembled to resist the Argive forces. Hyllus’s attendant reports that its chiefs are informed, its left wing is formed, and the troops are ready for battle after the victims have been removed from the ranks.

l: Argives, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The Argive army is led by Eurystheus and waits on a mountain ridge while its leader considers the safest route and position for an attack. It is close to the Athenian forces, and its approach causes the sacrifices and defenses of Athens to be set in motion.

l: the foreign suppliants, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The foreign suppliants are the children of Hercules, Iolaus, and Alcmena, who seek protection in Athens from Argos. Their presence places Athens in danger, but Demophoon and the Chorus argue that the city must not betray guests who have appealed for aid.

l: Argive invasion of Athens, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The battle between the Athenian and Argive forces is imminent when Hyllus marshals the troops. Iolaus insists that honor requires him to assist his friends, though the servant warns that his age and weakness make him unable to fight effectively.

l: Macaria’s sacrifice, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Macaria’s sacrifice is required by the oracles as the means of saving the city and the suppliants. She freely accepts this role, refuses to be chosen by lot, requests female attendants and proper rites, and departs to die for her brothers and Athens.

l: the threat to Athens, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: The threat to Athens comes from the approaching forces of Argos and Eurystheus. The city faces both foreign attack and possible civil conflict over whether to protect the suppliants, while the required sacrifice is presented as the means of averting destruction.

l: glory and reputation in war, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Macaria seeks honorable fame by dying willingly for her brothers rather than living as an abandoned and dishonored refugee. The Chorus says that her virtue will be praised in the grave, and Iolaus declares that her glory will surpass that of other women.

l: death, Hecuba and other plays, DEMOPHOON, IOLAUS, CHORUS.
s: Death is presented by Macaria as preferable to dishonor, abandonment, and captivity. She embraces a firm and voluntary death for a glorious cause, while Iolaus says that the wise have regarded death as the most effective cure for every ill.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The Servant reports to Alcmene that the allied forces have defeated the Argive army, while Hyllus and the rejuvenated Iolaus pursued and captured Eurystheus. Iolaus regained his youth temporarily through the favor of Hercules and Hebe and brought Eurystheus back alive. Alcmene demands Eurystheus's death, but the Messenger explains that Athens forbids killing a captive taken alive in battle. Eurystheus reveals an oracle of Phoebus promising that his buried corpse will protect Athens against the descendants of the race he hates, and Alcmene orders his execution.

l: Alcmena, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Alcmene learns from the Servant that her loved ones are alive, that the battle has been won, and that Iolaus has regained his youth. She confronts Eurystheus, accuses him of persecuting Hercules and his children, and insists that he die despite the decree of Athens. She orders her servants to kill him and cast out his corpse.

l: Servant, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The Servant tells Alcmene that the forces opposing Eurystheus have prevailed. He recounts Hyllus's challenge, the battle, Iolaus's rejuvenation, and the capture of Eurystheus, then asks Alcmene to fulfill her promise and set him free.

l: Messenger, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The Messenger brings Eurystheus before Alcmene and reports that Hyllus and Iolaus have captured him. He warns that the rulers of Athens forbid the killing of a captive taken alive in battle.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus celebrates the victory and the reversal of fortune, praises Zeus's justice, and says that Hercules now dwells among the gods with Hebe. It advises Alcmene to release Eurystheus because Athens desires it, but later approves her decision to have him killed.

l: Hyllus, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Hyllus challenges Eurystheus to single combat, offering to surrender the sons of Hercules if he is defeated and to claim his palace and hereditary rank if Eurystheus dies. When Eurystheus refuses, Hyllus returns to the ranks, fights successfully, and later joins Iolaus in raising trophies.

l: Iolaus, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Iolaus asks Hyllus to place him in his chariot, takes the reins, and pursues Eurystheus. After praying to Hebe and Zeus, he temporarily regains his youthful strength, captures Eurystheus near the rocks of Scyron, and brings him back alive.

l: Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Eurystheus refuses Hyllus's challenge and is defeated, captured, chained, and brought before Alcmene. He defends his actions as those of a threatened enemy, accepts that Athens spared him under its laws, and reveals an oracle stating that his buried corpse will protect Athens against the descendants of the race he opposed.

l: Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Hercules is said to dwell with the gods and to have appeared with Hebe as one of two stars above Iolaus's chariot. He is praised for his courage and deeds, while Eurystheus is accused of sending him into deadly labors and of persecuting his family.

l: Jove, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Zeus is invoked as the author of the victory and as a god whose judgments punish pride. Iolaus prays to Zeus for the temporary restoration of his youthful strength.

l: Argives, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The Argive army fights against the opposing forces, initially breaks through their lines, and later gives way. It is ultimately put to flight after a fierce battle.

l: Athenian army, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The Athenian army fights in defense of its land and reputation. Its forces help defeat the Argive army and contribute to the capture of Eurystheus.

l: children of Hercules, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The sons of Hercules are threatened by Eurystheus and have been driven from Greek states while seeking refuge at sacred altars. Their victory frees them from Eurystheus's rule and allows them to return to their father's city and inherit its fields.

l: Athens, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Athens defeats the forces led by Eurystheus and refuses to kill him because he was captured alive in battle. Eurystheus prophesies that his corpse, buried near the temple of the Pallenian maid, will become a guardian of Athens.

l: Argos, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Argos supplies the army that fights against Athens and the supporters of the sons of Hercules. Its people are urged by their commander to avoid disgrace and defend their native land.

l: Mycenae, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Mycenae is identified as the place from which Eurystheus led his forces. Its interests are invoked in Hyllus's proposed single combat, and its famous walls are described as having been built by the Cyclops.

l: Argive invasion of Athens, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The battle begins after single combat fails and a sacrificial virgin is killed as an auspicious victim. The armies clash with heavy losses, and the Athenian side eventually puts the Argive forces to flight.

l: single combat, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Hyllus proposes single combat with Eurystheus to settle the conflict and determine the fate of the sons of Hercules. Eurystheus refuses to face him, so the armies proceed to battle.

l: Iolaus's rejuvenation, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Iolaus's rejuvenation occurs after he prays to Hebe and Zeus while pursuing Eurystheus. Hercules and Hebe are seen as stars above his chariot, and Iolaus temporarily regains the strength of youth.

l: capture of Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: After the battle, the rejuvenated Iolaus pursues Eurystheus, seizes him in his chariot near the rocks of Scyron, binds him with chains, and brings him before Alcmene.

l: death of Eurystheus, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Alcmene orders Eurystheus to be killed in revenge for his crimes, despite Athens's rule against killing a captive taken alive. Eurystheus accepts that she may destroy him and says that his death will give Athens the protection foretold by the oracle.

l: oracle of Phoebus, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: The oracle of Phoebus declares that Eurystheus's corpse must be buried near the temple of the Pallenian maid. It promises that he will protect Athens after death and harm the descendants of the race he detests when they attack the city.

l: laws of Greece, Hecuba and other plays, SERVANT, ALCMENA, CHORUS.
s: Eurystheus argues that the laws of Greece protect a captive who was not killed during battle. The Messenger and Eurystheus both state that killing him after his capture would stain the person responsible with lasting guilt.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Hector learns from the Chorus of Trojan sentinels that the Greek camp is ablaze and in tumult during the night, possibly preparing to flee, but Aeneas advises sending a spy rather than attacking immediately. Dolon volunteers for the nocturnal spying mission in exchange for Achilles’ steeds and prepares to enter the Greek camp disguised as a wolf. A shepherd reports that Rhesus, son of Strymon, has arrived from Thrace with a large army, golden armor, and exceptionally white horses to aid Troy. Hector agrees to receive Rhesus as a friend and ally, although he initially scorns the late assistance.

l: Rhesus, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Rhesus, son of Strymon, is reported to have entered the fields of Troy with a large Thracian force. He travels in a chariot drawn by exceptionally white horses, wears resplendent golden armor, and comes to aid Troy.

l: Hector, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Hector is roused during the night by reports of unusual activity in the Greek camp and initially assumes that the Greeks are fleeing. After hearing Aeneas’s counsel, he agrees to send a spy and later welcomes Rhesus as a friend and ally, despite scorning his delayed assistance.

l: Aeneas, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Aeneas warns Hector that the fires in the Greek camp may be a stratagem and that a night attack could expose the Trojan troops to danger. He advises sending a voluntary spy and promises to support Hector if an attack becomes necessary.

l: Dolon, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Dolon volunteers to spy on the Greek fleet and agrees to undertake the mission in return for Achilles’ steeds. He boasts that he will return before sunrise, possibly after killing Ulysses or Diomede and bringing back one of their heads.

l: Chorus of Trojan sentinels, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The Chorus of Trojan sentinels wakes Hector and reports the fires, torches, and tumult in the Greek camp. It urges caution, approves Aeneas’s plan to send a spy, encourages Dolon, and celebrates the arrival of Rhesus.

l: the Trojan army, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The Trojan army is ordered to prepare its weapons when the Greek camp appears to be in motion. Hector later tells the troops to remain ready to follow the summons of the trumpet if the Greeks begin to flee.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The Greek army kindles fires throughout its camp and rushes toward Agamemnon’s tent during the night. Hector suspects that it is preparing to abandon the shore, while Aeneas warns that the activity may instead conceal a trap.

l: the Thracians, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The Thracian army arrives under Rhesus and is described as immense, with many horses, shield-bearing troops, archers, and infantry in Thracian dress. It has marched by night through the area around Ida to aid Troy.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Troy is presented as receiving Rhesus and his forces as allies. The Chorus hopes that Rhesus will save the threatened city and restore celebrations, while Hector believes Troy is already prospering in battle.

l: the Greek fleet, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The Greek fleet lies near the hostile shore, with torches and fires blazing on or near its ships. Dolon plans to approach its trenches and ramparts to discover the Greeks’ intentions.

l: Greek encampment, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The Greek camp is lit by numerous fires during the night, and its troops move tumultuously toward Agamemnon’s tent. Its unusual activity leads Hector to suspect a flight, but Aeneas considers that the fires may be intended to lure the Trojans into danger.

l: the Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The battle has favored Hector and the Trojans, and Hector believes the Greek defeat has created an opportunity to destroy the Greek ships. Aeneas cautions that a night engagement could become dangerous if the Greeks resist.

l: the Greek flight, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The Greek flight is suspected because fires blaze throughout the Greek camp and near the fleet. Hector is prepared to attack if the Greeks are departing, but the Chorus and Aeneas note that their actual intention has not yet been established.

l: the nocturnal spying mission, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: The nocturnal spying mission is proposed by Aeneas and undertaken by Dolon. Its purpose is to discover whether the Greeks intend to flee or to ensnare the Trojans.

l: Achilles’ steeds, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Achilles’ steeds are promised to Dolon as the reward for his spying mission. Hector describes them as descended from an immortal race and says that Neptune gave them to Peleus.

l: Dolon’s wolf disguise, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS.
s: Dolon’s wolf disguise consists of a tawny wolf hide, a hairy animal face covering, and arrangements for his hands and legs to imitate the beast’s movement. He intends to use it to approach the Greek trenches and ramparts without being discovered.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Rhesus arrives at Troy with Thracian forces and promises Hector that he will destroy the Greek fortifications and fleet in a single day. Hector rebukes Rhesus for coming late, while Rhesus explains that war with the Scythians delayed him and claims that he can end the siege. They discuss the Greek commanders, especially Achilles, Ajax, Tydeus’ son, and Ulysses, before Hector assigns Rhesus a place to encamp and gives Apollo as the watchword. After Rhesus departs, Hector orders the watch extended while the Chorus waits anxiously for Dolon, who was sent to reconnoitre the Greek fleet.

l: Rhesus, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Rhesus arrives at Troy with Thracian forces after being delayed by war with the Scythians. He promises to storm the Greek fortifications, burn their fleet, kill the Greeks, and return home the next day, and he claims he will seize Ulysses if he encounters him.

l: Hector, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Hector rebukes Rhesus for failing to come sooner despite Troy’s appeals and gifts, but acknowledges that Rhesus previously helped establish his throne. He assigns Rhesus a position in the army, gives Apollo as the watchword, and orders the watch to receive Dolon if he returns.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus praises Rhesus’s courage and prays that he will defeat the Greeks and redden the plain with their blood. During the night watch, it tracks the changing guards, wonders why Dolon has not returned, and fears that he may have been ambushed or killed.

l: Dolon, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Dolon has been sent by Hector to explore the Greek fleet. He has not yet returned as the Chorus expects, and his absence causes concern that he may have fallen into an ambush.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Troy has endured the Greek siege for ten years and has repeatedly sought aid from Rhesus. Hector hopes to preserve the city, while Rhesus promises to deliver it from the besieging forces.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The Argive host is the Greek force opposing Troy. Rhesus promises to storm its defenses and defeat it, while Hector identifies its leading warriors as Achilles, Ajax, Tydeus’ son, and Ulysses.

l: Phrygians, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The Trojans have continued fighting while the siege has lasted, and many of their allies have died or remain under arms. Hector tells them not to carry shields if Rhesus attacks the Greek fleet, trusting Rhesus’s spear to subdue the enemy.

l: the Thracians, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The Thracian host accompanies Rhesus to Troy after his campaign against the Scythians. Hector orders that Apollo be used as the watchword for the Thracian host in an emergency.

l: the Greek fleet, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The Greek fleet is the object of Rhesus’s immediate attack. He declares that he will burn it, while Dolon has been sent to reconnoitre it.

l: Trojan walls, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan walls are the defenses of the city that Rhesus promises to overthrow. Hector says that Rhesus may choose a position on the left wing, right wing, or centre near the front of the fighting.

l: Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The siege of Troy has continued ineffectually for ten years. Rhesus claims that his arrival will end the struggle quickly, but Hector cautions him not to focus on distant conquests while Troy’s immediate danger remains.

l: Rhesus’s arrival at Troy, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Rhesus’s arrival at Troy follows a delayed journey caused by war with the Scythians near the Euxine. He says that he crossed the Hellespont and marched through various lands without resting in luxury before reaching Troy.

l: Dolon’s reconnaissance, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Dolon’s reconnaissance concerns the Greek fleet and has kept him away from the Trojan lines. Hector and the Chorus await his report, but the unit ends before he returns.

l: night watch, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: The night watch changes according to assigned divisions, with different groups guarding the ramparts and Lycia’s warriors due to be roused. The Chorus notes that the night is ending as the Pleiades rise and dawn approaches.

l: the Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Battle is expected at once, with Rhesus promising to fight the Greeks and Hector offering him a place in the Trojan formation. Rhesus particularly seeks to confront the Greek forces and punish Ulysses, whom he condemns for stealth and sacrilege.

l: warfare and conquest, Hecuba and other plays, RHESUS, HECTOR, CHORUS.
s: Rhesus describes warfare and conquest as the means by which he will rescue Troy, seize Greek spoils, and later ravage Greece. Hector considers the conquest of Argos and the Greek states far less easy than Rhesus claims.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Ulysses and Diomede enter the Trojan camp at night, kill Rhesus and seize his chariot and white horses. Minerva directs them away from Hector and Paris, then helps them escape after the Trojan guards are alerted. Rhesus’s charioteer reports the destruction of the Thracian force and accuses Hector, while Hector blames Ulysses and condemns the guards. The Muse reveals Rhesus’s parentage, mourns him, and declares that he will be restored to life as a god, while Hector prepares Troy for battle at dawn.

l: Ulysses, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Ulysses enters the Trojan camp with Diomede, kills Rhesus, and takes Rhesus’s chariot and horses. He follows Minerva’s direction to withdraw, gives the watchword Apollo to the Trojan guards, and escapes with Diomede.

l: Diomede, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Diomede accompanies Ulysses into the Trojan camp and agrees to kill the Thracian soldiers while Ulysses seizes the horses. He escapes with Ulysses after Rhesus is slain.

l: Minerva, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Minerva directs Ulysses and Diomede to attack Rhesus rather than Hector or Paris, whom the Destinies forbid them to kill. She assumes Venus’ form to detain Paris, then warns Ulysses and Diomede that the Trojan guards have been alerted and urges them to flee.

l: Rhesus, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Rhesus arrives at Troy with numerous Thracian troops to aid the Trojans. Ulysses and Diomede kill him while he sleeps, and the Muse later declares that he will be restored to life as a god and priest of Bacchus.

l: Hector, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Hector places Rhesus and the Thracian troops outside the Trojan lines until morning. After Rhesus is killed, Hector angrily blames the Trojan guards, later disputes the charioteer’s accusation, promises care for the wounded man, and orders the dead to be buried with respect.

l: Paris, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Paris hears a report that enemies have entered the camp and goes to seek Hector. Minerva, appearing as Venus, reassures him and persuades him to return to his former station.

l: the Muse, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Muse appears carrying Rhesus’s body, identifies herself as one of the nine sisters, and mourns her son. She explains Rhesus’s divine and royal origins, blames Minerva for his fate while acknowledging that Ulysses and Diomede gave the wound, and prophesies Rhesus’s restoration to divine life.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Greeks have kindled fires around their ships, prompting the Trojan guards to believe that an attack may be imminent. Ulysses and Diomede, acting for the Greeks, enter the Trojan camp and kill Rhesus.

l: Trojans, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Trojans suffer the loss of Rhesus and his troops through the night raid. Hector orders them to proclaim the deaths, bury the slain, arm themselves, and await the trumpet signal for an assault on the Greek camp.

l: the Thracians, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Thracians arrive as allies of Troy, but their king and much of their force are destroyed during the night. Their charioteer survives with a wound and reports the disaster.

l: Chorus of Trojan sentinels, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Trojan guards fail to detect Ulysses and Diomede as they enter and leave the camp, and Hector threatens them with punishment or death. They later challenge the fugitives, but accept Ulysses after he gives the watchword Apollo.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Chorus first pursues the night raiders and debates whether Ulysses carried out the exploit. It then hears the charioteer’s account, witnesses the dispute with Hector, and responds to the Muse’s lament before preparing to obey Hector’s orders.

l: the charioteer of Rhesus, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Rhesus’s charioteer wakes to the sound of dying men, sees Rhesus bleeding, and is wounded while trying to find weapons. He survives, accuses Hector of murdering the Thracians for their horses, and is taken to Hector’s house for treatment.

l: Rhesus’s Thracian army, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Rhesus’s Thracian army is stationed outside the Trojan lines and sleeps without adequate sentinels or properly arranged arms. Ulysses and Diomede destroy the force’s leadership and leave the army utterly ruined.

l: the Trojan camp, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Trojan camp is entered by Ulysses and Diomede during the night. Rhesus’s troops are placed there, but the camp’s guards fail to prevent the raid and are later ordered to prepare for battle.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Troy is aided by Rhesus and the Thracians during the war with the Greeks, but the loss of Rhesus brings a reversal of fortune. Hector nevertheless hopes to storm the Greek ramparts, burn the fleet, and bring freedom to Troy.

l: the Greek fleet, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Greek fleet is threatened by Rhesus, whom Minerva says could destroy it if he survives the night. Hector later intends to storm the Greek ramparts and burn the fleet.

l: Rhesus’s car, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Rhesus’s car stands beside his sleeping place with the Thracian horses yoked to it. Ulysses and Diomede seize the car after killing Rhesus.

l: Rhesus’s white horses, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Rhesus’s white horses are described as having coats like swan feathers and as unmatched in beauty. Minerva directs Ulysses and Diomede to carry them away as a glorious prize, and the charioteer says that the raiders escaped with them.

l: Rhesus’s death, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Rhesus’s death occurs when Ulysses and Diomede attack his sleeping camp during the night. The Muse mourns it, Hector orders that his body be buried with honor, and the Muse declares that he will later be restored to divine life.

l: the Trojan night raid, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Trojan night raid is carried out by Ulysses and Diomede against Rhesus and the Thracians. It kills Rhesus, devastates his army, and ends with the raiders escaping through the alerted Trojan camp.

l: the Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: The Trojan War continues as the Greeks besiege Troy and Troy seeks aid from allied Thracian forces. The night attack on Rhesus intensifies the conflict, and Hector prepares a new assault against the Greek camp.

l: fate and the Destinies, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Fate and the Destinies prevent Ulysses and Diomede from killing Hector or Paris. The Muse says that fate ordained the deaths of Rhesus and his allies, and that an inevitable shaft will later bring death to Achilles.

l: Rhesus’s funeral and apotheosis, Hecuba and other plays, ULYSSES, DIOMEDE.
s: Hector orders that Rhesus and the other dead be interred with due respect, while he plans to honor Rhesus with a tomb and rich garments. The Muse says that Rhesus will not remain in an ordinary grave but will be restored to life as a god, priest of Bacchus and of the deity worshipped beneath Pangaeum.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Neptune and Minerva agree to punish the Greeks for Ajax’s violation of Minerva’s temple by sending storms against their homeward voyage. Hecuba learns from Talthybius that the Trojan captives have been assigned to Greek lords: Cassandra to Agamemnon, Andromache to Achilles’ son, Hecuba to Ulysses, and Polyxena to Achilles’ tomb. Cassandra arrives in ecstatic prophetic frenzy, treating her enslavement to Agamemnon as a wedding and foretelling the destruction of his house and the sufferings of the Greeks. Talthybius leads Cassandra away, while Hecuba and the chorus mourn Troy’s destruction and their enslavement.

l: Neptune, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Neptune leaves the ruined Troy after recalling how Apollo and he built its towers. He agrees with Minerva to raise storms, waves, and whirlpools against the returning Greeks in punishment for the profanation of the gods’ shrines.

l: Minerva, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Minerva seeks Neptune’s aid against the Greeks because Ajax tore Cassandra from her temple and escaped punishment. She plans to make the Greek homeward voyage disastrous, with Zeus’s thunderbolts and Neptune’s storms.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Hecuba mourns the destruction of Ilion, the deaths of Priam and her sons, and her own enslavement. Talthybius tells her that Ulysses has won her by lot, while Cassandra has been assigned to Agamemnon and Andromache to Achilles’ son.

l: Cassandra, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Cassandra enters carrying a bridal torch and celebrates her supposed marriage to Agamemnon, though she prophesies that she will destroy him and that the Atreus house will fall. She predicts Ulysses’ long and perilous return, foretells her own death, and leaves with Talthybius.

l: Andromache, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Andromache, the captive wife of Hector, has been chosen by Achilles’ son.

l: Talthybius, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Talthybius announces the results of the captives’ assignments to Hecuba and the chorus. He is ordered to deliver Cassandra to Agamemnon’s hands and then leads her toward the fleet.

l: Menelaus, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Menelaus is named as the leader whose wife Helen caused the Greeks to come against Troy. Hecuba wishes to remain enslaved to Menelaus in order to meet the perfidious Helen.

l: Helen, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Helen is described as the Spartan woman whose abduction led to the Greek expedition and as an adulteress hated by Hecuba. She is among those the Greeks have taken captive and is associated with the destruction of Priam, his sons, and Hecuba.

l: Agamemnon, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Agamemnon has taken Cassandra as his chosen prize and intends to make her his concubine. Cassandra prophesies that she will destroy his palace and that his house will suffer ruin.

l: Ulysses, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Ulysses has won Hecuba by lot. Cassandra prophesies that he will spend ten additional years away from home, face many dangers at sea and abroad, and encounter countless troubles after reaching his house.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The chorus of captive Trojan dames fears the judgment assigning each woman to a Greek master and mourns the loss of Troy, their homes, their marriages, and their children. It joins Hecuba in lamentation and questions the fate awaiting the captives.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The Grecian host has sacked Troy, divided its captives by lot, and waits for favorable winds before sailing home. Minerva and Neptune resolve to punish it with storms and destruction at sea.

l: Trojans, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The Trojans have lost their city and many of their people in the Greek assault. Cassandra argues that the Trojans who died in battle received burial in their native land, while the Greeks who fell were left far from their families.

l: gods, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The gods’ deserted temples and violated sacred places are presented as causes for divine anger. Minerva and Neptune arrange divine punishment for the Greeks, and Cassandra speaks as Apollo’s inspired priestess.

l: Ilion, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Ilion has been destroyed, its towers overthrown, its temples polluted, and its smoke rising into the sky. Its surviving women are held captive, while its dead include Priam, his sons, and Polyxena.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Troy is described as once prosperous and protected by its temples and towers, but it has been laid waste by the Greeks after ten years of war. Neptune mourns its ruined shrines, and Cassandra claims that the Trojans’ fate is in some respects happier than that of the victorious Greeks.

l: the sack of Troy, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Troy’s fall has left its royal family dead, its women enslaved, and its sacred places profaned. Hecuba and the chorus lament the city’s destruction, while Minerva and Neptune connect the Greeks’ future punishment with their treatment of Troy.

l: Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The Trojan War is described as a ten-year Greek assault undertaken to recover Helen. Cassandra condemns the war for the lives it consumed and contrasts the suffering of the Greek dead and their families with the honors given to fallen Trojans.

l: lottery assigning the captives, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The lottery assigning the captives determines separate Greek masters for the Trojan women. Cassandra goes to Agamemnon, Andromache to Achilles’ son, Hecuba to Ulysses, and Polyxena to Achilles’ tomb.

l: Cassandra’s relationship with Agamemnon, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Cassandra’s enslavement to Agamemnon is announced as her assignment as his concubine rather than as an ordinary slave. She responds by performing a mock bridal celebration and prophesying that the union will bring disaster to Agamemnon and his house.

l: Polyxena’s sacrifice, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Polyxena’s sacrifice at Achilles’ tomb is reported to Hecuba as her assigned fate. Talthybius calls Polyxena fortunate because death releases her from the afflictions suffered by the surviving captives.

l: Greek homeward voyage, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The Greek homeward voyage is prepared after the captives have been assigned and the fleet has received its plunder. Minerva and Neptune intend to make the voyage disastrous through thunder, violent winds, waves, and shipwreck.

l: Cassandra’s prophecy, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Cassandra’s prophecy foretells Agamemnon’s destruction, the fall of the Atreus house, her own death, and Ulysses’ prolonged and perilous journey home. She also predicts that the Greeks will suffer more deeply than the Trojans despite their victory.

l: Achilles’ tomb, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Achilles’ tomb is the place where Polyxena has been assigned to minister. Hecuba initially misunderstands the assignment as service for sepulchral rites before learning that Polyxena’s fate is death.

l: Agamemnon’s tent, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: Agamemnon’s tent stands in the Greek camp near Troy and serves as the place where Hecuba and the captive women are held. Talthybius comes from it to announce the captives’ assignments.

l: the Greek fleet, Hecuba and other plays, THE TROJAN CAPTIVES.
s: The Greek ships wait near Troy to carry the victorious host and the captive women away. Cassandra asks where the general’s ship is, while Minerva and Neptune prepare storms to destroy or scatter the fleet.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Hecuba mourns the destruction of Troy, the deaths of her family, and her own impending enslavement in Greece. Andromache arrives with Astyanax and learns from Talthybius that the Greeks have decreed her son must be thrown from Troy’s towers because he is Hector’s child. Andromache laments Astyanax’s impending death, while Hecuba and the Chorus mourn Polyxena’s sacrifice, Hector’s death, and the fall and sack of Troy. The Chorus recounts how the Greeks deceived the Trojans with the wooden horse and destroyed their city.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Hecuba laments that she was born to regal state, married Priam, bore valiant sons, and lost Priam, her sons, her daughters, and her city. She expects to be carried to Greece as an aged slave, performing degrading labor, and mourns Cassandra, Polyxena, Hector, and Astyanax. She advises Andromache to submit to Neoptolemus and preserve Astyanax, but then learns that the Greeks have ordered the boy’s death.

l: Andromache, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Andromache is taken away by the Greeks with Astyanax and the spoils of Hector. She tells Hecuba that Polyxena was sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles and that her own fate as a captive forced into Neoptolemus’ household is worse. She grieves over Astyanax after Talthybius announces that he will be thrown from Troy’s towers.

l: Astyanax, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Astyanax, the son of Hector and Andromache, is the only one of Andromache’s loved ones remaining in Troy. The Greeks decree that he must be thrown from the towers because they will not allow the son of Hector to grow up. Andromache gives him a final embrace and kiss before he is taken away.

l: Hector, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Hector is remembered as the bravest of the Phrygians, a noble husband, and the father of Astyanax. He was killed, and his death leaves Andromache captive and Astyanax condemned because of his paternal fame.

l: Polyxena, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Polyxena is dragged to the tomb of Achilles and killed as a gift to the deceased. Andromache saw her bleed, covered her body with a shroud, and mourned her; Hecuba considers death preferable to the suffering endured by the living.

l: Talthybius, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Talthybius reluctantly tells Andromache that the Greeks have decreed Astyanax’s death. He says Ulysses persuaded the assembled Greeks that the son of Hector must not be raised, and he urges Andromache not to resist if she wants her son to receive funeral honors.

l: Neoptolemus, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Neoptolemus, the son of Achilles, takes Andromache as a captive and resolves to make her his wife. He is associated with the spoils taken from Troy and with the household into which Andromache is forced.

l: Ulysses, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Ulysses persuades the assembled Greeks that Astyanax, as the son of Hector, must not be allowed to grow up. His argument leads to the decree that Astyanax be thrown from the towers of Troy.

l: gods, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Hecuba invokes the gods while admitting that she finds no firm allies in them. She says the gods have poured such torrents of suffering upon her that her tongue is unable to express it, and the Chorus attributes Troy’s ruin to the will of angry Heaven. The Chorus also presents the gods as false in relation to Troy’s destruction.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Chorus supports Hecuba, mourns Troy, and sings odes about the wooden horse, the destruction of the city, and the suffering of its inhabitants. It describes the Greeks’ deception, the slaughter within Troy, the enslavement of the survivors, and the grief of women who lose children and husbands.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Greeks deceive Troy with the wooden horse, storm the city, kill its defenders, enslave its women, and carry away its spoils. They sacrifice Polyxena and decree that Astyanax be killed. Their leaders also threaten punishment if Andromache resists.

l: Trojans, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Trojans bring the wooden horse through their gates and place it in Minerva’s temple, believing it to be a holy pledge of peace. They celebrate while the Greeks concealed inside it emerge and begin the destruction of Troy.

l: Ilion, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Troy, also called Ilion and Pergamus, is captured, burned, and leveled by the Greeks. Its royal houses, temples, streets, altars, and customs are destroyed, and its surviving women and children are carried into slavery or death.

l: Greece, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Greece is the destination to which Hecuba, Andromache, and the other captive Trojan women are taken. Andromache is to serve there in Neoptolemus’ household, while Talthybius says Greece may grant funeral honors to Astyanax if she remains silent.

l: the Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Trojan War is represented through the destruction of Troy, the deaths of Trojan youths, and the enslavement of the surviving women. The Chorus recalls earlier Greek attacks on Troy and the final deception by the wooden horse.

l: the fall and destruction of Troy, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The fall of Troy leaves Hecuba without her husband, children, city, or freedom. It is portrayed as the result of the Greeks’ wooden-horse deception, followed by slaughter, fire, captivity, and the loss of the Trojan royal house.

l: the sack of Troy, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The sack of Troy includes the Greeks’ entry from the wooden horse, the killing of Trojan youths, the desecration of altars, and the destruction of the city. The survivors are forced into servitude, while Trojan women mourn their dead and are taken away.

l: the Trojan Horse, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Trojan Horse is a wooden vehicle containing armed Greeks and disguised with splendid trappings. The Trojans mistake it for a sacred pledge of peace, bring it inside the gates, and thereby admit the force that destroys Troy.

l: Achilles’ tomb, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The tomb of Achilles is the place where Polyxena is taken and killed. Her death is presented as a gift to the deceased Achilles.

l: Polyxena’s sacrifice, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Polyxena’s sacrifice occurs at the tomb of Achilles, where she bleeds and dies by impious hands. Andromache witnesses the death, covers Polyxena with a shroud, and says Polyxena’s fate is more enviable than that of the living captives.

l: Astyanax’s execution, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Astyanax’s execution is ordered by the Greeks after Ulysses argues that Hector’s son must not be raised. He is to be thrown from the towers of Troy, and Andromache gives him a final farewell before he is taken away.

l: Hector’s death, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Hector’s death leaves Andromache widowed and Astyanax without his father’s protection. His fame as a heroic defender becomes the reason the Greeks condemn his son.

l: the enslavement of Hecuba and the Trojan women, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Trojan women’s enslavement follows the destruction of Troy. Hecuba, Andromache, and the other women are carried to Greece and assigned degrading or forced roles in the households of their Greek masters.

l: the Phrygian matrons, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Trojan women mourn the dead, the destruction of their city, and the loss of their husbands and children. They are carried away as captives to Greece, where they face servitude and separation from their families.

l: the bridal marriage of Paris and Helen, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The marriage associated with Paris and Helen is blamed for Troy’s suffering. Hecuba says that through one woman’s nuptials she has borne dreadful ills, and the Chorus calls Paris’ espousals accursed.

l: the Trojan royal house, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The Trojan royal house is destroyed through the deaths of Priam, Hector, the royal sons, and the royal daughters. Hecuba, once queen, is reduced to an aged slave, while Astyanax is killed before he can inherit or rebuild Troy.

l: the wooden horse deception, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: The wooden horse deception causes the fall of Troy. The Greeks conceal armed men inside the wooden structure, while the Trojans bring it into the city as a sacred offering and celebrate without recognizing the trap.

l: hope, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Andromache says that hope visits other sufferers but never comes to her, because no promised joy remains. Hecuba says that fair hope cannot be entirely extinguished while life remains, though her own circumstances leave little room for it.

l: fate and the Destinies, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Fate is described as uncontrolled and capable of reducing noble birth to slavery. Hecuba and Andromache’s sufferings are presented as the result of devastating vicissitudes that overturn prosperity.

l: grief and mourning, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Grief and mourning dominate the speeches and songs of Hecuba, Andromache, and the Chorus. They mourn the dead, the burning city, the loss of family, and the separation of mothers from children; tears and lamentation are described as a relief to sufferers.

l: slavery, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Slavery is the fate awaiting Hecuba, Andromache, and the other surviving Trojan women after the city’s destruction. Their noble birth offers no protection, and they are assigned to degrading service or forced relationships in Greece.

l: death, Hecuba and other plays, CHOR. Attendants of the aged Hecuba,
s: Death takes Priam, Hector, the Trojan sons, Polyxena, and many Trojan youths. Andromache says death is preferable to a life of misery, while Hecuba reflects that the dead no longer suffer or weep.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus arrives at the ruined Troy to take Helen to Greece, intending that she eventually be slain for the deaths and suffering caused by the war. Helen defends herself by blaming the Judgment of Paris, Venus, Paris, and forces beyond her control, while Hecuba rejects her arguments and accuses her of willingly abandoning Menelaus for wealth and luxury. Menelaus accepts Hecuba’s accusation and orders Helen taken to the ships, though he agrees that she will not enter his own vessel. The Chorus mourns the destruction of Troy, the loss of its religious rites, and the suffering of the Phrygian women, and prays that Helen never reaches Greece.

l: Menelaus, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus comes to Troy to reclaim Helen and says that he fought not merely for a woman but to punish Paris for violating hospitality. He resolves that Helen will be taken to Greece and killed, but after Hecuba’s warning he agrees that Helen will not enter his own ship.

l: Helen, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Helen is dragged from the tents and allowed to answer the accusations against her. She claims that Venus, Paris, Priam, and divine compulsion caused her ruin, and says that Deiphobus forced her into marriage after Paris died. Menelaus accepts Hecuba’s judgment against her and orders her taken to the ships for execution in Greece.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba asks Menelaus to hear Helen’s defense but then refutes it. She argues that Helen willingly followed Paris because of his beauty and Troy’s wealth, rejected Hecuba’s advice to flee, and continued to display pride rather than remorse. She urges Menelaus to kill Helen as punishment for the deaths of the Greeks and her children.

l: Paris, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Paris is described as the cause of the disasters after he judged the three goddesses. Helen says that he came to Menelaus’s house with Venus and took her away, while Hecuba says that Helen willingly loved him after seeing his beauty and wealth.

l: Venus, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Venus allegedly promised Paris that she would give him Helen if he awarded her the prize of beauty. Helen blames Venus for making her leave Sparta, while Hecuba argues that Venus was only a name for Helen’s own desire.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus urges Helen to defend her children and country against Helen’s persuasive speech and supports Hecuba’s demand for punishment. In its ode, it mourns Troy’s ruined shrines, lost sacrifices, dead defenders, and the suffering caused by Helen’s marriage.

l: the Grecian host, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Grecian host destroys Paris and Troy and entrusts Helen’s fate to Menelaus, allowing him either to spare her or to take her away. Menelaus says that the host came to punish the violation of hospitality.

l: the Greeks, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Greeks wage war against Troy, destroy the city, and suffer deaths before its walls. Helen claims that her marriage benefited the Greeks by keeping them from barbarian rule, but Hecuba and Menelaus hold her responsible for their losses.

l: Phrygians, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Phrygians are the people of Troy whose city is destroyed by the Greek army. Hecuba says that the Phrygians disapproved when Deiphobus took Helen by force, and the Chorus mourns the slaughter and enslavement of the Phrygian women.

l: women, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Women are presented as subject to a proposed law that any woman who betrays her husband should die. Menelaus says that Helen’s ruin should warn all women to be chaste.

l: Troy, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Troy has been destroyed by the spear and fire of the Greeks, and its religious sanctuaries, sacrifices, and citadel lie ruined. Its surviving women are captives, while its dead, including Astyanax, are mourned.

l: Greece, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Greece is the destination to which Menelaus intends to convey Helen. The Chorus mourns the Greek losses caused by the war and describes Helen’s marriage as a disgrace to Greece and its allied states.

l: the Trojan War, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Trojan War is presented as the consequence of Paris’s violation of hospitality and Helen’s connection with him. It has resulted in the destruction of Troy, the deaths of Greeks and Trojans, and the enslavement of Trojan women.

l: the judgment of Paris, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Judgment of Paris is described as the contest in which Paris awarded the prize of beauty to Venus over Juno and Minerva. Helen says that Venus then promised him Helen as his reward, while Hecuba rejects this account as an excuse for Helen’s conduct.

l: the sack of Troy, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The fall of Troy is shown through the city’s destruction, the loss of its temples and rites, the deaths of its people, and the enslavement of its women. The Chorus also recalls that Greece threw Astyanax from the city’s towers.

l: Helen’s defense, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Helen’s defense claims that divine influence, Paris, Priam, and force rather than her own will caused her departure from Sparta and her life in Troy. She also says that she tried to escape after Paris’s death but was prevented by the guards and later forced into marriage by Deiphobus.

l: Hecuba’s accusation of Helen, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba’s accusation states that Helen willingly chose Paris because of his beauty and Troy’s wealth, remained in Paris’s household by choice, and followed Fortune rather than virtue. Hecuba says that Helen refused repeated advice to flee and shows no remorse for the war.

l: hospitality, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus and Hecuba treat Helen’s death as justice for the deaths and suffering caused by the war. Menelaus proposes that her punishment should serve as a warning to all women who betray their husbands.

l: Fortune, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Helen attributes her actions to Venus and to Heaven’s decrees, claiming that her crime was compelled and therefore venial. Hecuba rejects this explanation, while the Chorus asks whether Jove will hear Troy’s lament and questions the divine cause of its destruction.

l: Helen’s execution, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus first says that Helen will be stoned or killed in Greece to atone for the woes of Greece. He orders her taken to the ships and later states that she will be slain in Argos, although she will not travel in his own vessel.

l: Greek homeward voyage, Hecuba and other plays, MENELAUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Menelaus intends to carry Helen across the sea to Greece, where she is to be killed. The Chorus imagines the voyage as a miserable transport from Troy and prays that lightning will destroy the ship before Helen reaches Sparta.

l: Hecuba and other plays, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Talthybius tells Hecuba that Neoptolemus has sailed for Phthia with Andromache and has entrusted Astyanax’s body to Hecuba for burial. Hecuba mourns Astyanax, condemns the Greeks for killing him, and buries him in Hector’s shield after performing funeral rites with the Chorus. Talthybius then orders the burning of Troy and tells Hecuba that she must follow Ulysses into slavery. Hecuba and the Chorus lament the flames, the destruction of Troy, and their removal from their homeland.

l: Talthybius, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Talthybius tells Hecuba that Neoptolemus has departed for Phthia with Andromache and has left Astyanax’s body in Hecuba’s care. He says that he washed the body and will help mark out and dig the grave, then later orders the Greek troops to burn Troy and commands Hecuba to follow Ulysses.

l: Hecuba, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hecuba mourns over Astyanax’s mutilated body, adorns it with the poor gifts available to her, and performs his funeral rites. She condemns the Greeks for killing a child, laments the destruction of Troy, and is taken into slavery under Ulysses.

l: Chorus, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus helps prepare Astyanax’s funeral ornaments and joins Hecuba in lamentation. It witnesses and describes the burning and destruction of Troy and shares Hecuba’s grief at being driven from the homeland.

l: Astyanax, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Astyanax has been thrown from the walls of Ilion and killed by the Greeks because they feared that he might someday rebuild Troy. His disfigured body is brought to Hecuba for burial, and he is interred in Hector’s shield.

l: Neoptolemus, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Neoptolemus hears that his grandsire Peleus has suffered recent evils and that Acastus has expelled Peleus from his realm, so he departs swiftly for Phthia. He takes Andromache with him and permits Astyanax’s body to be given to Hecuba for burial.

l: Andromache, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Andromache leaves the land with Neoptolemus, lamenting her country and addressing her plaints to Hector’s tomb. She entrusts Astyanax’s body to Hecuba because Neoptolemus’s haste prevents her from burying him herself.

l: Hector, Hecuba and other plays, TALTHYBIUS, HECUBA, CHORUS.
s: Hector is remembered as Astyanax’s father and as the former possessor of the shield in which Astyanax is buried. Hecuba recalls Hector’s sweat and likeness impressed on the shield and says that he will complete in the shades what remains unfinished for Astyanax.
